From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia \"Francia\"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun \"Treaty of Verdun\") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* (\"king of the Franks\"), *rex Francorum orientalium* (\"king of the East Franks\"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the \"Germans\", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor\") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus \"Theodiscus\"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans \"King of the Romans\"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added \"king in Germany\" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity\\'s sake)\\n2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany \"Kingdom of Germany\") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector \"Prince-elector\"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 \"Golden Bull of 1356\") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)\\n3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title \"emperor\" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy \"Iron Crown of Lombardy\"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy \"King of Italy\"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor\") by the pope.\\n4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor\") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor\") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor\") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor\\'s lifetime.\\n\\nEmperors are listed in **bold**. titles\")]\\n\\n1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia \"Francia\"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun \"Treaty of Verdun\") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* (\"king of the Franks\"), *rex Francorum orientalium* (\"king of the East Franks\"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the \"Germans\", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor\") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus \"Theodiscus\"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans \"King of the Romans\"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added \"king in Germany\" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity\\'s sake)\\n2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany \"Kingdom of Germany\") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector \"Prince-elector\"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 \"Golden Bull of 1356\") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)\\n3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title \"emperor\" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy \"Iron Crown of Lombardy\"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy \"King of Italy\"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor\") by the pope.\\n4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor\") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor\") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor\") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor\\'s lifetime.\\n\\nEmperors are listed in **bold**. titles\")]\\n\\n1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia \"Francia\"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun \"Treaty of Verdun\") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* (\"king of the Franks\"), *rex Francorum orientalium* (\"king of the East Franks\"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the \"Germans\", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor\") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus \"Theodiscus\"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans \"King of the Romans\"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added \"king in Germany\" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity\\'s sake)\\n2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany \"Kingdom of Germany\") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector \"Prince-elector\"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 \"Golden Bull of 1356\") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)\\n3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title \"emperor\" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy \"Iron Crown of Lombardy\"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy \"King of Italy\"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor\") by the pope.\\n4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor\") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor\") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor\") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor\\'s lifetime.\\n\\nEmperors are listed in **bold**. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia \"Francia\"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun \"Treaty of Verdun\") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* (\"king of the Franks\"), *rex Francorum orientalium* (\"king of the East Franks\"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the \"Germans\", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor\") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus \"Theodiscus\"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans \"King of the Romans\"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added \"king in Germany\" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity\\'s sake)\\n2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany \"Kingdom of Germany\") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector \"Prince-elector\"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 \"Golden Bull of 1356\") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)\\n3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title \"emperor\" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy \"Iron Crown of Lombardy\"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy \"King of Italy\"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor\") by the pope.\\n4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor\") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor\") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor\") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor\\'s lifetime.\\n\\nEmperors are listed in **bold**. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

East Francia (843–962)
----------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: East Francia (843–962)")]

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

1. **[^](#cite_ref-16)** He was crowned in [Aachen Cathedral](/wiki/Aachen_Cathedral "Aachen Cathedral") by the [Archbishop of Cologne](/wiki/Archbishop_of_Cologne "Archbishop of Cologne") in 1257, campaigned in the Rhineland with his German allies to liberate the elector of Cologne, organised the [Diet of Worms of 1269](/w/index.php?title=Diet_of_Worms_of_1269&action=edit&redlink=1 "Diet of Worms of 1269 (page does not exist)") and married in the same year in [Kaiserslautern](/wiki/Kaiserslautern "Kaiserslautern") with [Beatrice of Falkenburg](/wiki/Beatrice_of_Falkenburg "Beatrice of Falkenburg"), but only resided in Germany in 1257, 1258, 1260, 1262, 1263, 1268 and 1269. He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").

Note on titles
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Note on titles")]

1. The Kingdom of Germany started out as the eastern section of the [Frankish kingdom](/wiki/Francia "Francia"), which was split by the [Treaty of Verdun](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") in 843. The rulers of the eastern area thus called themselves *rex* *Francorum* ("king of the Franks"), *rex Francorum orientalium* ("king of the East Franks"), and later just *rex*. A reference to the "Germans", indicating the emergence of a German nation of some sort, did not appear until the late eleventh century, when the pope began to refer to his enemy [Henry IV](/wiki/Henry_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor") as *rex teutonicorum*, king of the [Germans](/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus"), in order to brand him as a foreigner. The kings reacted by consistently using the title *rex Romanorum*, [king of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans"), to emphasize their universal rule even before becoming emperor. This title remained until the end of the Empire in 1806, though after 1508 emperors-elect added "king in Germany" to their titles. (Note: in this and related entries, the kings are called *kings of Germany*, for clarity's sake)
2. The [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") was never entirely hereditary; rather, ancestry was only one of the factors that determined the succession of kings. During the 10th to 13th centuries, the king was formally elected by the leading nobility in the realm, continuing the Frankish tradition. Gradually the election became the privilege of a group of princes called [electors](/wiki/Prince-elector "Prince-elector"), and the [Golden Bull of 1356](/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1356 "Golden Bull of 1356") formally defined election proceedings.[[23]](#cite_note-25)
3. In the Middle Ages, the king did not assume the title "emperor" (from 982 the full title was *Imperator Augustus Romanorum*, Venerable Emperor of the Romans) until crowned by the pope. Moving to Italy, he was usually first crowned with the [Iron Crown of Lombardy](/wiki/Iron_Crown_of_Lombardy "Iron Crown of Lombardy"), after which he assumed the title of *rex Italiae*, [king of Italy](/wiki/King_of_Italy "King of Italy"). After this, he would ride on to Rome and be [crowned emperor](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor") by the pope.
4. [Maximilian I](/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor") was the first king to bear the title of emperor-elect. After his march to Rome for his Imperial coronation failed in 1508, he had himself proclaimed emperor-elect with papal consent.[[24]](#cite_note-26) His successor [Charles V](/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") also assumed that title after his coronation in 1520 until he was crowned emperor by the pope in 1530. From [Ferdinand I](/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") onwards, all emperors did not get crowned by the Pope anymore. At the same time, chosen successors of the emperors held the title of king of the Romans, if elected by the college of electors during their predecessor's lifetime.

Emperors are listed in **bold**. Rival kings, anti-kings, and junior co-regents are *italicized*.

He remained in England during the [Second Barons' War](/wiki/Second_Barons%27_War "Second Barons' War") in support of his brother and spent a period during the years 1264 and 1265 in the captivity of the English barons. The remainder of his reign he resided in England.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about monarchs ruling over Germany after the 843 Treaty of Verdun. For ancient German/Germanic kings before the treaty, see [List of Frankish kings](/wiki/List_of_Frankish_kings "List of Frankish kings"). For German monarchs who lost their thrones in 1918, see [List of German monarchs in 1918](/wiki/List_of_German_monarchs_in_1918 "List of German monarchs in 1918").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/HRR_10Jh.jpg/250px-HRR_10Jh.jpg)](/wiki/File:HRR_10Jh.jpg)

German kingdom (blue) in the Holy Roman Empire around 1000

This is a list of monarchs who ruled over [East Francia](/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), and the [Kingdom of Germany](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Germany "Kingdom of Germany") ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Regnum Teutonicum*), from [the division](/wiki/Treaty_of_Verdun "Treaty of Verdun") of the [Frankish Empire](/wiki/Francia "Francia") in 843 and [the collapse](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Holy_Roman_Empire "Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire") of the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") in 1806 until [the collapse](/wiki/German_Revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German Revolution of 1918–1919") of the [German Empire](/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") in 1918:

Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)
----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_monarchs_of_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Holy Roman Empire (962–1806)")]

The title "[King of the Romans](/wiki/King_of_the_Romans "King of the Romans")", used in the [Holy Roman Empire](/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), denoted a ruler elected by the German princes whose authority was primarily exercised over the Germanic-speaking territories of the empire. While no formal “King of Germany” existed, the king’s election and governance effectively corresponded to that of a monarch over these lands. After election, the king would traditionally proceed to Rome to be [crowned emperor by the pope](/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor").
